intro: Turkish culture blends Central Asian, Persian, Arab, Byzantine and European influences, from grand mosques and bazaars to kebabs, Turkish delight and TV dramas watched across the world.

chapters.title: Food and drink
text: Turkish cooking includes kebabs of every kind, mezes (small shared dishes), stuffed vegetables, simit (sesame bread rings) and sweets such as baklava and Turkish delight. A Turkish breakfast spreads cheese, olives, tomatoes, eggs, honey and bread across the table.
Turkish coffee, boiled in a small pot and served with the grounds, is on UNESCO's heritage list; some people read fortunes in the leftover grounds.

chapters.title: Mosques, palaces and bazaars
text: The Ottoman architect Mimar Sinan designed hundreds of buildings in the 1500s, including Istanbul's Süleymaniye Mosque. The Blue Mosque, Topkapı Palace, where sultans lived, and Hagia Sophia, a church, then a mosque, then a museum and since 2020 a mosque again, are nearby.
The Grand Bazaar, begun in the 1400s, is one of the oldest and largest covered markets in the world, with thousands of shops selling carpets, lamps, jewellery and spices.

chapters.title: Arts and stories
text: The Mevlevi, followers of the poet Rumi, perform the Sema, a spinning ceremony; they are known in English as whirling dervishes. Ebru, the art of marbling paper by floating paint on water, and Iznik tiles with blue and red flowers are famous crafts.

Orhan Pamuk won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2006. The jokes of Nasreddin Hodja, a wise fool, are told across the Middle East and Central Asia, and Turkish TV dramas are exported to more than a hundred countries.
